newsitem.title: Slovenia: Slovenia strong entrant for next NATO round - U.S..
newsitem.headline: Slovenia strong entrant for next NATO round - U.S..

text.p: The United States on Saturday told Slovenian leaders disappointed at their country's exclusion from the first round of NATO expansion that there was "no stronger candidate" than Slovenia for the second round.

"If Slovenia does stay on the track that it has established...there is no stronger candidate for membership in the next round than Slovenia," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said after talks in the former Yugoslav republic.

A NATO summit in Madrid on Tuesday invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to become the first ex-communist countries to apply for membership, despite pressure from France and other allies to include Romania and Slovenia as well.
The summit communique mentioned Bucharest and Ljubljana as promising future candidates, but Albright's comments on Saturday were the strongest suggestion so far that Slovenia would get in next time.

Following the summit, U.S. President Bill Clinton, Defence Secretary William Cohen and Albright have been visiting Central and East European states to explain the Madrid decision, which was taken at U.S. prompting.

After meeting Slovenian President Milan Kucan and Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek, Albright told a news conference that in order to be sure of membership, Slovenia must continue its present course of democratic and economic reforms.

Slovenian Foreign Minister Zoran Thaler told the news conference his country "in a way was disappointed that it was not admitted in the first round" but accepted Albright's assurances. He congratulated the three invited countries.

Slovenia and Croatia headed the drive to break up the former Yugoslavia by declaring independence in 1991, but unlike Croatia, Slovenia, an Alpine state of less than two million people, managed to stay out of the ensuing Balkan conflict.

Albright said Slovenia had made major progress toward meeting NATO standards "given its strong, stable democracy and relatively developed economy" and had "made a solid start in developing a small but capable military".

But she said that NATO was still looking for a more non-partisan foreign policy, further economic reforms to encourage foreign investment, more modernisation of its armed forces and a greater role in regional peace-keeping.
NATO "is not an escape hatch from our common troubles in the Balkans; it means taking responsibility for the security of others just as others take responsibility for your security," she said.

Despite its attraction to NATO strategists as a land bridge between existing member Italy and prospective member Hungary, Slovenia has not yet restructured its armed forces from being a territorial defence backup to the Yugoslav army.
Its professional troops currently stand at only 4,100 although conscripts serving seven-month military service terms swell the number to some 56,000.
Thaler said his government felt the armed forces were "the proper size" but was striving to meet NATO standards.
President Kucan told a separate news conference later that Slovenia would press ahead to meet requirements to be included in Western institutions.

"The main task of Slovenia is to continue to work in the direction of reforms in order to qualify as a serious NATO candidate and to be included in the first round of members of the European Union," he said.

U.S. officials said that both in Slovenia and Romania they had found a desire by leaders to obtain U.S. advice on how to comply with NATO demands, despite predictions by experts that excluded countries would feel isolated and bitter.
"Rather than bemoaning their fate, they wanted to look to the future," one official said.
